_comment: GENERATED by tools/build_monographs.py — do not hand-edit. Descriptive reference text only: no dosing guidance, and approval status never gates logging. NOT clinically reviewed — on the pre-ship checklist for owner review.

monographs.summary: Water-soluble B vitamin. The one whose upper limit is easiest to exceed accidentally, because it appears in multivitamins, B-complexes and greens powders at once.
monographs.body: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine, or pyridoxal-5-phosphate in activated products) is involved in amino acid metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis. Deficiency is uncommon on a normal diet.
monographs.commonUses: Included in most multivitamins and B-complex products; sometimes taken for premenstrual symptoms or morning sickness.
monographs.safetyNotes: Sustained intake above the upper limit is associated with peripheral neuropathy — numbness and tingling in the hands and feet — which is usually but not always reversible on stopping. This is the single most common accidental supplement overexposure, and it happens by stacking products rather than by taking too much of any one of them.

monographs.summary: Fat-soluble vitamin. Preformed retinol accumulates; beta-carotene does not.
monographs.body: Vitamin A covers two different things: preformed retinol from animal sources and supplements, and provitamin carotenoids from plants. Only preformed retinol counts toward the upper limit, because the body regulates how much carotene it converts.
monographs.commonUses: Vision, immune function, skin. Common in multivitamins and cod liver oil.
monographs.safetyNotes: Preformed vitamin A is stored in the liver and accumulates. High intake in pregnancy is associated with birth defects. Cod liver oil, a multivitamin and a skin supplement taken together can exceed the limit without any single product looking excessive.

monographs.summary: Essential mineral. Its upper limit applies only to supplements — dietary magnesium is not counted against it.
monographs.body: Magnesium is involved in several hundred enzymatic reactions. Supplemental forms differ considerably in how much elemental magnesium they contain and how well it is absorbed: oxide is about 60% magnesium by weight but poorly absorbed, glycinate about 14% but better tolerated.
monographs.commonUses: Sleep, muscle cramps, constipation (citrate and oxide), general repletion.
monographs.safetyNotes: The most common effect of too much supplemental magnesium is diarrhoea, which is self-limiting. The 350 mg upper limit refers to supplemental intake only.
monographs.contraindications: Reduced kidney function — magnesium clearance depends on it.

monographs.summary: Essential mineral. Accidental overdose is a leading cause of poisoning in young children.
monographs.body: Iron supplements vary in elemental content by form — ferrous fumarate is about 33% iron, gluconate about 12%, so 'equal' doses on two labels can differ threefold.
monographs.safetyNotes: Iron is a common cause of accidental poisoning in children; supplements should be stored out of reach. Supplementing without a documented deficiency is not benign — iron is not readily excreted.

monographs.summary: Fat-soluble vitamin, stored in the body. Widely supplemented, and easy to over-supply when several products contain it.
monographs.body: Vitamin D is measured in both micrograms and IU: 100 mcg is 4,000 IU. Products label it inconsistently, which is a frequent source of accidental double-dosing.
monographs.safetyNotes: Being fat-soluble, it accumulates. Sustained very high intake can raise blood calcium.

monographs.summary: B vitamin. The upper limit applies to synthetic folic acid, not to folate from food.
monographs.body: Folate from food and synthetic folic acid from supplements and fortified grain behave differently, which is why the limit distinguishes them.
monographs.safetyNotes: High folic acid intake can mask the anaemia of vitamin B12 deficiency while the neurological damage continues.

monographs.summary: B vitamin. High doses cause a distinctive and harmless-feeling flush that is often mistaken for a reaction.
monographs.body: The upper limit applies to synthetic niacin from supplements and fortified food, not to niacin occurring in food.
monographs.offLabelUses: High-dose niacin has been used for lipid management under supervision.
monographs.safetyNotes: Doses above the limit commonly cause flushing; sustained very high intake has been associated with liver injury.

monographs.summary: Trace mineral with a narrow window between adequate and excessive.
monographs.body: Selenium's upper limit is only about five times a typical adequate intake — one of the narrowest margins among the minerals. Brazil nuts alone can approach it.
monographs.safetyNotes: Chronic excess causes selenosis: hair and nail brittleness or loss, garlic breath odour, gastrointestinal upset.

monographs.summary: Essential mineral. Competes with copper for absorption.
monographs.safetyNotes: Sustained supplemental zinc above the upper limit can induce copper deficiency, which presents as anaemia and neurological symptoms and is easily missed.

monographs.summary: Pain reliever and fever reducer. The leading cause of acute liver failure in the US, and about half of poisonings are unintentional.
monographs.body: Acetaminophen (paracetamol outside the US) appears in a very large number of combination products: cold and flu remedies, sleep aids, and prescription opioid combinations. Because the name on the front of the box is rarely 'acetaminophen', people stack it without knowing.
monographs.safetyNotes: Roughly 40% of unintentional acute-liver-failure cases involved two or more acetaminophen-containing products taken together. Check every product label. Alcohol increases the risk of liver injury at a given dose.
monographs.contraindications: Existing liver disease; regular heavy alcohol use.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Approved and available over the counter.

monographs.summary: NSAID pain reliever.
monographs.safetyNotes: NSAIDs carry gastrointestinal bleeding and kidney risks that rise with dose and duration, and combining two different NSAIDs multiplies the risk without adding benefit.
monographs.contraindications: Peptic ulcer disease; significant kidney impairment; late pregnancy.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Approved and available over the counter.

monographs.summary: Stimulant. Present in coffee, tea, energy drinks and a great many pre-workout and fat-burner supplements at the same time.
monographs.body: Caffeine is the substance most often double-counted, because supplement sources are invisible next to dietary ones — a pre-workout, a fat burner and two coffees add up quickly.
monographs.safetyNotes: Around 400 mg a day is a commonly cited ceiling for healthy non-pregnant adults. Pure powdered caffeine has caused deaths from measuring error.
monographs.contraindications: Pregnancy — lower limits apply. Some arrhythmias.
monographs.typicalHalfLife: About 5 hours, longer in pregnancy and with some medications

monographs.summary: Herbal antidepressant with an unusually large number of drug interactions.
monographs.body: St John's Wort induces the CYP3A4 enzyme system and P-glycoprotein, which speeds up the clearance of many medicines and can reduce them to ineffective levels.
monographs.safetyNotes: It reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives, some HIV and cancer medicines, warfarin, ciclosporin and others. Combined with SSRIs it can contribute to serotonin excess. This is the herbal most worth checking against a medication list.
monographs.contraindications: Concurrent use with any prescription medication without checking interactions.

monographs.summary: Liver-supportive botanical.
monographs.commonUses: Commonly taken for liver support; also used alongside other supplements for that reason.
monographs.safetyNotes: Generally well tolerated. Evidence for benefit in liver disease is mixed.

monographs.summary: Adaptogenic botanical, most often taken for stress and sleep.
monographs.commonUses: Stress, sleep, and in some products for exercise performance.
monographs.safetyNotes: Case reports of liver injury exist, uncommon but documented. It may affect thyroid hormone levels and interacts with sedatives.

monographs.summary: Plant alkaloid, often taken for blood-sugar and lipid effects.
monographs.offLabelUses: Frequently taken for metabolic effects; sometimes described as a natural comparator to metformin, though the comparison is loose.
monographs.safetyNotes: Berberine inhibits CYP3A4 and can raise levels of other medicines. Gastrointestinal upset is common at higher intakes.

monographs.summary: Whole licorice root. Its glycyrrhizin content is what the safety story is about; deglycyrrhizinated (DGL) products are a separate, safer entry.
monographs.body: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra) contains glycyrrhizin (glycyrrhizinic acid), the compound responsible both for its characteristic sweetness and for its principal risk. This entry covers the whole root; products sold as DGL have had glycyrrhizin removed and are tracked separately.
monographs.commonUses: Traditionally taken for digestive complaints, sore throat and coughs; appears in many herbal blends and teas.
monographs.safetyNotes: Glycyrrhizin can cause pseudohyperaldosteronism: raised blood pressure, low potassium, fluid retention, and in severe cases heart-rhythm problems. EFSA advises staying below about 100 mg of glycyrrhizinic acid per day. That figure bounds the COMPOUND, not the root: measured glycyrrhizin content varies as much as 30-fold between products and is often not stated on the label, which is why this app attaches no numeric limit to licorice root — a threshold in mg of root would be wrong by an unknown factor either way. Regular intake, sensitive individuals, and anyone with hypertension, heart or kidney disease should treat whole-root products cautiously. DGL products do not carry this risk.
monographs.contraindications: Hypertension; heart failure; kidney disease; low potassium; pregnancy. Concurrent diuretics, digoxin or corticosteroids.

Danish market survey of glycyrrhizin content
NCCIH: Licorice Root

monographs.summary: One of the most studied sports supplements.
monographs.commonUses: Strength and power performance; increasingly studied for cognitive effects.
monographs.safetyNotes: Well tolerated in healthy people. Causes a small increase in body water early on. Raises measured creatinine, which can be mistaken for a kidney problem on a blood test — mention it to whoever ordered the test.

monographs.summary: Hormone involved in sleep timing.
monographs.safetyNotes: Supplement products commonly contain far more than is needed, and label accuracy has been found to be poor in independent testing. Timing matters more than amount for circadian effects.

monographs.summary: Amino acid derivative; the precursor to glutathione.
monographs.commonUses: Antioxidant and liver support; a prescription form is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose.
monographs.safetyNotes: Generally well tolerated.

monographs.summary: Synthetic pentadecapeptide. Not an approved medicine anywhere; the human evidence base is very thin and most published work is in animals.
monographs.body:
BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid sequence said to derive from a protein found in gastric juice. It has no marketing approval from any regulator, and the interesting thing about it is not the pharmacology but the shape of its evidence base, which several independent sources characterise the same way.

A 2025 systematic review in orthopaedic sports medicine screened 544 records published between 1993 and 2024 and included 36 studies: 35 preclinical and one clinical. It found no clinical safety data at all. Reviewers examining the wider literature note that the great majority of records - by one count over 80% of everything indexed under the name - carry the same Croatian group, led by Predrag Sikiric, as authors, and that experiments there routinely test a single dose rather than a range. Independent replication is close to absent, which is the specific gap that matters: a result reproduced only by the people who first reported it is not yet a result. A published 2025 exchange in Pharmaceuticals, where Sikiric's group replied to a critical review and the review's authors replied in turn, is worth knowing about because it shows the disagreement is live inside the literature rather than only between enthusiasts and sceptics.

The regulatory record runs alongside. The FDA placed BPC-157 in Category 2 of the interim 503A bulk substances list in September 2023 - the category for substances needing further evaluation on safety or efficacy grounds - and its compounding status has been moving since. In sport, WADA does not name it among specific compounds; it is caught by category S0, non-approved substances, which prohibits at all times anything no health authority has approved for human therapeutic use. That is a broader prohibition than being named, not a narrower one.

Read together, the sources agree on the facts and differ mainly in tone. Nothing here says the compound does not work. It says that after three decades the question has not been asked in a way that could answer it, and that anyone taking it is relying on animal data, one group's reporting, and material from an unregulated supply chain.
monographs.offLabelUses: Discussed for tendon, ligament and gut healing. All such use is unapproved.
monographs.safetyNotes: No approved medicine contains it, so material is obtained outside the regulated supply chain, where identity, purity and sterility are not assured. Long-term safety in humans is unstudied.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not FDA-approved. Removed from the FDA compounding Category 2 list on 2026-04-22; a Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee review was scheduled for 2026-07-23/24. Status is actively changing.

monographs.summary: Synthetic peptide related to thymosin beta-4. Not approved for human use; prohibited in sport.
monographs.body:
TB-500 is routinely described as thymosin beta-4, and the single most useful thing to know about it is that those are two different molecules. Thymosin beta-4 is the natural 43-amino-acid protein present in nearly every mammalian cell. TB-500 is a synthetic seven-residue fragment, Ac-LKKTETQ, corresponding to residues 17 to 23 - the actin-binding region. The fragment is not the protein, and the distinction decides which evidence applies to which.

It matters because the good human data belongs to the parent. RegeneRx developed full-length thymosin beta-4 as an eye drop under the designation RGN-259 and ran real trials: a phase 2 in 72 people with moderate-to-severe dry eye reported reduced discomfort scores and improved corneal staining against placebo over 28 days, and a phase 3 in neurotrophic keratitis reported complete corneal healing in a majority of treated patients. Those are ophthalmic trials of the whole protein delivered to the eye. A 2026 scoping review of thymosin beta-4 and TB-500 in tissue healing found no registered human trial of the seven-residue fragment for any musculoskeletal indication - every human number in circulation belongs to the parent peptide, and usually to a different route and a different tissue.

WADA is unambiguous and, unlike BPC-157, names it directly: the 2026 prohibited list's S2 section covers thymosin-beta-4 and its derivatives, giving TB-500 as the worked example, prohibited at all times both in and out of competition. There is no approved human medicine containing it, so material sold under the name comes from outside the regulated supply chain, where identity, concentration and sterility are not verified by anyone.

The honest summary is that the mechanism is real biology, the clinical evidence is for a different molecule, and the transfer from one to the other is an assumption rather than a finding.
monographs.offLabelUses: Discussed for soft-tissue and tendon recovery. Unapproved.
monographs.safetyNotes: Prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency. Sourced outside regulated channels, with the purity and sterility uncertainty that implies.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not approved for human use.

monographs.summary: Growth-hormone secretagogue. Not an approved medicine; available through compounding pharmacies in the US.
monographs.body:
Ipamorelin is a synthetic growth hormone secretagogue - a pentapeptide acting at the ghrelin receptor to prompt the pituitary to release its own growth hormone, rather than supplying growth hormone directly. Its selling point in the literature is selectivity: compared with earlier GHRPs it produces comparatively little effect on cortisol and prolactin, which is a genuine pharmacological distinction and is most of why it stayed interesting.

What it does not have is a completed clinical programme. It was investigated commercially and development did not lead to an approved product, so there is no approved labelling anywhere, and therefore no verified indication, no established long-term safety profile, and no authoritative contraindication or interaction list. This is the part most consumer writing skips: the absence of a label is not a bureaucratic gap, it is the absence of the document against which every other safety claim would be checked.

Three regulatory sources describe the same trajectory from different angles. The FDA placed ipamorelin acetate in Category 2 of the interim 503A bulk substances list in September 2023; it was then removed in September 2024, but on the specific ground that the parties who nominated it withdrew their nominations - a procedural withdrawal, not a finding that it is safe or effective, and a distinction widely misreported as the FDA clearing it. WADA lists ipamorelin by name in the 2026 prohibited list under S2, among growth hormone secretagogues and their mimetics, prohibited at all times. And no comparable regulator elsewhere has approved it either.

It is often combined with a GHRH analogue such as CJC-1295, on the theory that the two act on different receptors and stack. No human randomised trial of that combination has been published, so the pairing is a mechanistic argument rather than a tested one.
monographs.offLabelUses: Discussed for recovery, body composition and sleep. Unapproved.
monographs.safetyNotes: Growth-hormone axis effects are not benign; they influence blood glucose and fluid balance. Long-term data are lacking.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not FDA-approved as a drug. Remains in compounding Category 1, so compounding pharmacies may prepare it.

sources.name: FDA 503A bulk drug substances, Category 2 update
FDA removes certain peptide bulk drug substances from Category 2
WADA Prohibited List, S2 growth hormone secretagogues

monographs.summary: Growth-hormone-releasing hormone analogue. Not approved for human use.
monographs.body:
CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone releasing hormone. Two versions circulate under the same name, which is the first thing to get straight: the original carried a drug affinity complex that binds albumin and extends its life in the body for days, while the version usually sold now is the plain modified peptide, sometimes distinguished as CJC-1295 without DAC. A source describing one is not describing the other, and much of the confusion in circulation comes from that.

Its measurable pharmacology is documented. A single dose of the long-acting form has been reported to raise growth hormone two- to tenfold, with the effect persisting six days or more, and IGF-1 one-and-a-half to threefold. Those are real published measurements, and they are measurements of a hormone level rather than of an outcome anyone cares about - no trial has followed that through to body composition, injury recovery or anything else in a controlled human population, and no randomised trial of the common CJC-1295-plus-ipamorelin pairing has been published at all.

The regulatory record is unusually explicit for a research peptide. CJC-1295 was placed in Category 2 of the FDA's interim 503A bulk substances list in 2023 and removed in September 2024 on nominator withdrawal. In December 2024 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee reviewed it directly and recommended against including its forms on the 503A Bulks List, with most forms voted down unanimously; FDA compounding safety material cites limited clinical data, immunogenicity, impurities and reports of serious adverse reactions. WADA's 2026 list names CJC-1295 explicitly under S2 as a GHRH analogue, alongside CJC-1293, sermorelin and tesamorelin, prohibited at all times.

So three bodies have examined it and none concluded in its favour: it has documented endocrine activity, no demonstrated clinical benefit, an advisory committee that voted against it, and a standing ban in sport.
monographs.offLabelUses: Discussed alongside secretagogues for growth-hormone effects. Unapproved.
monographs.safetyNotes: Product identity is unusually inconsistent under this name. Growth-hormone axis effects influence glucose metabolism.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not FDA-approved.

FDA 503A bulk drug substances, Category 2 update

monographs.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonist. An approved medicine, prescribed for type 2 diabetes and for weight management under different brand names.
monographs.body:
Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist and one of the few compounds in this section that is a fully approved medicine with a public label, which changes what can be said about it: the statements below come from regulatory documents and completed phase 3 trials rather than from mechanism.

It is approved in the United States under more than one brand for more than one purpose. Ozempic was approved in December 2017 for type 2 diabetes, with the label expanded in January 2020 to include cardiovascular risk reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes and known heart disease. Wegovy, a separate higher-strength weekly presentation, is approved for long-term weight management and, since March 2024, for reducing the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity - the first medicine to carry both indications. An oral formulation also exists. The brand names are not interchangeable and their indications differ.

The cardiovascular claim rests on SELECT, a multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 17,604 adults across 41 countries who had established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity but no diabetes. It reported a 20% reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction and non-fatal stroke against placebo on top of standard care, with a 15% reduction in cardiovascular death and a 19% reduction in death from any cause. A separate analysis of the same trial published in Nature Medicine reported the weight trajectory over four years. That is an outcome trial with hard endpoints, which is a different and stronger class of evidence than the surrogate measures most peptides here rest on.

Two practical cautions. Compounded and grey-market semaglutide is a live problem, and concentration errors in unlabelled material are a documented cause of accidental overdose with this drug class. And because it is a real medicine with a real label, that label - not this entry - is where contraindications, warnings and interactions are recorded.
monographs.offLabelUses: Compounded and grey-market semaglutide is widely sold; these are not the approved product and concentration errors have caused documented dosing accidents.
monographs.safetyNotes: Gastrointestinal effects are common, particularly when the dose increases. Approved labelling carries a boxed warning regarding thyroid C-cell tumours observed in rodents. Pancreatitis has been reported.
monographs.contraindications: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: FDA-approved as a prescription medicine (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus).

Yale Medicine: why a cardiologist may prescribe semaglutide

monographs.summary: Dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist. An approved prescription medicine.
monographs.body:
Tirzepatide is a dual agonist, acting at both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors, and like semaglutide it is an approved medicine with published labelling rather than a research compound.

It holds three separate FDA approvals under two brand names, which is worth keeping straight because they are not the same product on paper. As Mounjaro it was approved in May 2022 for type 2 diabetes. As Zepbound it was approved in November 2023 for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related comorbidity. And in December 2024 Zepbound was approved for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with obesity - the first medicine approved for that condition. Mounjaro does not carry the sleep apnoea indication; the molecule is the same and the approvals are not.

The evidence behind each indication is a named phase 3 programme. SURPASS covered type 2 diabetes and SURMOUNT covered obesity; the sleep apnoea approval rests on SURMOUNT-OSA, a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnoea and obesity, run in two arms - those unable or unwilling to use positive airway pressure, and those continuing on it. It met its primary endpoint on change in the apnoea-hypopnoea index and its key secondary endpoints, with treated participants averaging up to about 20% weight reduction and at least 25 fewer breathing interruptions per hour of sleep; at one year roughly 42% on tirzepatide alone, and 50% on tirzepatide plus PAP, reached remission or mild non-symptomatic disease.

The same supply-chain caution applies as to semaglutide. Material obtained outside a pharmacy is not the labelled product, and dosing errors from mis-stated concentration are a recognised hazard across this whole drug class.
monographs.offLabelUses: Compounded versions are widely sold and are not the approved product.
monographs.safetyNotes: Gastrointestinal effects are common during dose escalation. Approved labelling carries a boxed warning regarding thyroid C-cell tumours observed in rodents.
monographs.contraindications: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: FDA-approved as a prescription medicine (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

sources.name: FDA approves Zepbound for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea
SURMOUNT-OSA phase 3 results
FDA approves tirzepatide as first treatment for OSA with obesity

monographs.summary: Investigational triple agonist (GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors). Not approved anywhere; still in clinical trials.
monographs.body:
Retatrutide is an investigational single molecule that activates three receptors - GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon - where the approved incretin drugs act on one or two. The glucagon component is the genuinely new element, and the reason both its effect sizes and its open safety questions are larger.

Its evidence base moved substantially through 2025 and 2026, so any older summary is out of date. The phase 3 TRIUMPH programme has now reported: TRIUMPH-4 read out in December 2025 with weight reduction up to 28.7% at 68 weeks; TRANSCEND-T2D-1 in type 2 diabetes reported in March 2026; the pivotal obesity trial TRIUMPH-1, an 80-week study in adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition and without diabetes, reported in May 2026 with all three doses meeting primary and key secondary endpoints and reductions reported up to 30.3%; and TRIUMPH-2 and TRIUMPH-3 reported together in July 2026. Lilly has stated an intended FDA submission in the first quarter of 2027, covering obesity and supported by work in obstructive sleep apnoea and knee osteoarthritis.

None of that is approval. There is no approved product, no approved labelling, and therefore no verified contraindication list, no interaction data and no established long-term safety profile - a distinction that matters more here than usual, because trial-grade efficacy results tend to be read as though they settled safety, and they do not. Effects of the glucagon-receptor arm on heart rate and on blood glucose are still being characterised.

Anything sold under this name today is not a licensed medicine and comes from outside the regulated supply chain, with identity, concentration and sterility unverified. Concentration error is a documented cause of accidental overdose in this class, and an investigational compound with no label is the worst case for it.
monographs.offLabelUses: Material sold under this name is not an approved medicine and is obtained outside the regulated supply chain.
monographs.safetyNotes: There is no approved labelling, so no verified safety information, contraindication list or interaction data exists. Identity, concentration and sterility of grey-market material are unverified, and concentration errors are a documented cause of accidental overdose with this class. Effects of the glucagon-receptor component on heart rate and blood glucose are still being characterised in trials.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Investigational. Not approved by the FDA or any comparable regulator. The phase 3 TRIUMPH programme has reported; the manufacturer has stated an intended FDA submission in Q1 2027. Submission is not approval, and no approved labelling exists.

monographs.summary: Growth-hormone-releasing factor analogue. Approved for one specific indication.
monographs.body:
Tesamorelin is a growth hormone releasing factor analogue, and it is the one compound in this group that reached full approval for the kind of body-composition purpose the others are marketed for - which makes it a useful reference point for what that evidence bar actually looks like.

The FDA approved it on 10 November 2010, as Egrifta, to reduce excess visceral abdominal fat in adults with HIV who have lipodystrophy. It remains the only medicine approved in the United States for that purpose, and it was the first FDA approval of a GHRH analogue for any adult indication. Rather than supplying growth hormone it stimulates the pituitary to release the body's own, which is the same mechanistic idea sermorelin and CJC-1295 rest on - the difference is that this one completed the trials.

The formulation has changed more than once and the brands are not one product: Egrifta, then Egrifta SV, and more recently an F8 formulation approved as Egrifta WR, which replaces Egrifta SV and moves reconstitution from daily to weekly. Prescribing information for these is published in the FDA's own document archive, and that label - not a summary - is the authoritative source for warnings and contraindications. Independent work has continued around it, including reports on visceral fat and liver fat in people with HIV on integrase-inhibitor regimens.

Two limits are worth stating plainly. The approval is narrow: it is for a specific complication in a specific population, and it is not an approval for body recomposition in healthy adults, which is what it is usually discussed for. And WADA's 2026 list names tesamorelin explicitly under S2 as a GHRH analogue, prohibited at all times - being an approved medicine does not make a substance permitted in sport.
monographs.offLabelUses: Used off-label for body composition more generally.
monographs.safetyNotes: Affects glucose metabolism; blood sugar warrants monitoring.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: FDA-approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy (Egrifta).

monographs.summary: Growth-hormone-releasing hormone analogue, formerly an approved product.
monographs.body:
Sermorelin is a synthetic 29-amino-acid fragment of growth hormone releasing hormone - the shortest sequence that retains the parent hormone's activity - and it prompts the pituitary to release its own growth hormone rather than supplying any.

Its regulatory history is the unusual part, and it is frequently told wrongly. It was approved in the United States, but as a diagnostic agent for assessing growth hormone deficiency in children, and that approval was subsequently withdrawn. It was not withdrawn on a safety finding, and it was never an approval for adult growth hormone therapy or for body composition. What followed was widespread use through compounding pharmacies for adult indications it had never been approved for, which is the status most people encounter it in today: available, prescribed, and unapproved for the purpose it is prescribed for.

That gap is why the compounding-regulation story matters here. FDA activity around 503A bulk drug substances from 2023 onward swept in a large group of peptides for exactly this reason - substances in real clinical use without the evidence package an approval would have required. Sermorelin's own human evidence for adult use is correspondingly thin: what exists documents that it raises growth hormone and IGF-1, which is the mechanism working, not an outcome demonstrated.

In sport it is not ambiguous. WADA's 2026 prohibited list names sermorelin explicitly in section S2 among GHRH analogues, alongside CJC-1293, CJC-1295 and tesamorelin, prohibited both in and out of competition.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: No longer marketed as an approved US product; available via compounding.

monographs.summary: Peptide developed in Russia, used there as a nootropic. Not approved in the US or EU.
monographs.body:
Semax is a synthetic peptide derived from a fragment of ACTH, modified so that it no longer carries the parent hormone's effect on cortisol. It is discussed for cognition and neuroprotection, and its position is genuinely unusual: it is simultaneously an approved pharmaceutical and an unapproved research chemical, depending entirely on where you are standing.

In Russia it is a registered medicine and has been on the national Vital and Essential Drugs list since 2011. Outside Russia no major regulator - not the FDA, not the EMA - has approved it for anything. The two facts are often presented as though one contradicts the other. They do not: they reflect different evidentiary standards, and the second is the one that describes what is known to Western review.

The evidence base is heavily Russian-language and heavily mechanistic. A PubMed search returns on the order of 150 records, a large share of them animal work on mechanism, with sparse English-language clinical data. Reviewers describe a mixed picture on quality: some Russian trials are properly controlled and blinded, others fall short of what the FDA or EMA would require; sample sizes are small by Western standards; and treatment periods run weeks to months rather than years, so chronic-use safety is essentially uncharacterised. There is also no Western sponsor with a commercial reason to fund the trials that would settle it, and the compound is largely unpatented outside Russia, so that is unlikely to change on its own.

For anyone obtaining it outside Russia, the practical consequence is that the approved product and the material actually purchased are not the same thing: the latter comes from unregulated research-chemical suppliers, where identity and purity are established by nobody.
monographs.safetyNotes: Little safety data outside its country of origin.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not FDA-approved; approved in Russia for specified indications.

monographs.summary: Peptide developed in Russia, used there for anxiety. Not approved in the US or EU.
monographs.body:
Selank is a synthetic peptide based on tuftsin, a naturally occurring immune-active fragment, extended for stability. It is discussed as an anxiolytic without the sedation or dependence associated with benzodiazepines. Its situation closely parallels Semax, and the two are usually described together for that reason.

Like Semax it is a registered medicine in Russia and unapproved everywhere else. It has one additional wrinkle in the United States: Selank acetate, listed as TP-7, was placed in Category 2 of the FDA's interim 503A bulk drug substances list and then removed in September 2024. That removal is routinely cited as though the FDA cleared it. It did not - the removal happened because the parties who had nominated it withdrew their nominations, which ends a review rather than concluding it. Withdrawal and clearance are different events with different meanings, and only one of them happened.

The clinical evidence carries the same limitations as Semax: predominantly Russian, small trials, short durations, and little independent Western replication. Nothing in that body of work meets the threshold the FDA or EMA would need to open a regulatory review, which is why no review is open. Long-term safety in humans is not characterised, and no approved labelling exists outside Russia to record contraindications or interactions.

Material bought outside Russia comes through research-chemical channels, with no verification of identity, concentration or sterility.
monographs.safetyNotes: Little safety data outside its country of origin.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not FDA-approved; approved in Russia.

monographs.summary: Copper-binding tripeptide, used mainly in topical cosmetic products.
monographs.body:
GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring copper-binding tripeptide, glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine complexed with copper, present in human plasma and declining with age. It has around forty years of published research, which is unusual for this list - but that research is overwhelmingly about one route of administration, and that is the distinction the entry turns on.

Topically, the evidence is real and comparatively deep: controlled work on wound healing, collagen synthesis in human skin, hair follicle effects and gene expression, including a 2002 photoaging trial and a more recent topical gel study reporting increased skin collagen density at three months. It is a small, water-soluble peptide and, in an appropriate formulation, reaches the dermis. Topical copper peptides are cosmetic products with a long commercial history.

Injectable GHK-Cu is a different proposition and should not inherit that evidence. No published human randomised trial has evaluated injected GHK-Cu for cosmetic, hair or wound endpoints, and no long-term safety trial of the injectable route exists; the protocols circulating are extrapolation from topical and preclinical work rather than findings. It is not FDA-approved for any injectable use, and it belongs in a separate risk category from the topical cosmetic products that share its name - which is precisely the inference most marketing invites and no source supports.

One further consideration is specific to this molecule: it delivers copper, an element the body regulates tightly and can accumulate. That is a reason for caution about systemic administration which does not arise for peptides that are only amino acids.
monographs.offLabelUses: Injected use for tissue repair. Unapproved.
monographs.safetyNotes: Copper-containing; relevant if other copper sources are also being taken.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Permitted in cosmetics; not approved as an injectable medicine.

monographs.summary: Synthetic tetrapeptide with almost no published human data.
monographs.body:
Epitalon is a synthetic tetrapeptide, Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly, designed to reproduce the active fragment of epithalamin, a pineal extract. It was characterised by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, and it is discussed for telomerase activation, sleep and lifespan.

The mechanistic literature is not empty. Work in rat pinealocytes reports upregulation of AANAT and pCREB, consistent with a direct effect on melatonin synthesis, and a study in elderly humans reported that pineal peptide preparations including epithalamin restored the nocturnal melatonin peak with a corresponding improvement in subjective sleep. Peer-reviewed reviews published in 2025 describe its bioactivity in some detail.

The problems are of two kinds and both are worth stating. The first is replication: the longevity claims rest largely on animal work from Khavinson's own group, and independent Western replication is minimal - the same structural weakness as BPC-157, from a different country and a different decade. The second is that the preclinical evidence actually conflicts. Synthetic epitalon and the natural extract are not established as equivalent, and a summary prepared for researchers by the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation notes that epithalon failed to stimulate melatonin production in rats while being reported to increase it in older primates. That is not a small discrepancy in a compound whose best-supported claim is about melatonin.

Beyond that: the sleep effect has not been tested in a controlled human trial, long-term human safety is unknown, no regulator has approved it, and material is obtained through unregulated suppliers.
monographs.offLabelUses: Discussed for longevity. Unapproved and unstudied in humans at any scale.
monographs.safetyNotes: No meaningful human safety data.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not approved anywhere.

monographs.summary: Mitochondrial-derived peptide. Preclinical only.
monographs.body:
MOTS-c is a mitochondrial-derived peptide - encoded in mitochondrial rather than nuclear DNA - and is usually described as an exercise mimetic. That label comes from preclinical work showing that administering it reproduces several metabolic adaptations of aerobic training without the training, largely through the AMPK pathway, shifting cells toward fat oxidation and improved glucose handling. The biology is well-founded and genuinely interesting.

The human evidence is where it stops. There are no completed large-scale human clinical trials for any therapeutic claim. The closest thing to a clinical programme was CohBar's analogue CB4211, which in a phase 1 trial showed acceptable tolerability and reported reductions in liver enzyme markers in obese subjects with fatty liver disease - after which development was discontinued, and no MOTS-c-based compound has since entered phase 2. A discontinued phase 1 analogue is not a foundation for the claims made about the parent peptide.

Reviewers list the specific gaps rather than gesturing at them. Human pharmacokinetics are not established, so absorption, distribution and clearance of subcutaneous administration are unknown; no dose-ranging trial has identified a therapeutic window in humans; delivery of mitochondrial-derived peptides remains a recognised technical barrier to clinical translation; and long-term human safety data is essentially absent, early tolerability notwithstanding.

The fair reading is that the preclinical evidence is robust and translation to humans is unproven - and that 'exercise mimetic' names a signalling pathway, not a demonstrated substitute for exercise.
monographs.offLabelUses: Discussed for metabolic and exercise effects. Unapproved.
monographs.safetyNotes: No human safety data.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not approved anywhere.

monographs.summary: Melanocortin receptor agonist. Approved for one specific indication.
monographs.body:
Bremelanotide, widely sold under its development code PT-141, is a melanocortin receptor agonist and - unlike most compounds in this section - an approved medicine with a label, which makes it one of the few where efficacy and safety statements rest on regulatory review.

The FDA approved it in June 2019 as Vyleesi, for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women. It was the second approved pharmacological treatment for that condition after flibanserin in 2015, and the first approved for on-demand rather than daily use. The scope is narrow and specific: HSDD means persistently low sexual desire causing personal distress that is not explained by another condition or by a medication, and the approval is for premenopausal women. It is not approved for men, for erectile dysfunction, or for general libido - all uses it is widely marketed for.

Mechanistically it is unlike the PDE5 inhibitors it gets compared with. Those act on blood vessels; bremelanotide acts centrally, at melanocortin receptors - chiefly MC3R and MC4R - in the hypothalamus and connected regions. It is given subcutaneously in advance of activity rather than on a schedule.

Its adverse-effect profile is documented rather than inferred. Nausea is the most common, followed by flushing, injection-site reactions and headache. Transient increases in blood pressure with accompanying decreases in heart rate have been observed, which is the finding most relevant to anyone with cardiovascular disease and the one most often omitted from consumer material. As with any approved medicine the current prescribing information is authoritative, and material obtained outside a pharmacy is not that product.
monographs.commonUses: Hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women.
monographs.offLabelUses: Used off-label by men and outside the approved indication.
monographs.safetyNotes: Nausea is common. It transiently raises blood pressure and lowers heart rate.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: FDA-approved for one indication (Vyleesi).

monographs.summary: Fragment of human growth hormone. Tested for obesity and did not show the hoped-for effect.
monographs.body:
AOD-9604 is a 16-amino-acid fragment of human growth hormone, corresponding to part of its C-terminal region, developed on the hypothesis that the fat-metabolising activity of growth hormone could be separated from its growth-promoting and glucose effects. It is marketed for fat loss. Its distinguishing feature is that, unlike most peptides here, it was properly tested - and the test is why it is not a medicine.

The early signal looked reasonable. A 12-week phase 2a trial in roughly 300 participants reported modest weight reduction, about 2.6 kg against 0.8 kg on placebo. Metabolic Pharmaceuticals then ran a 24-week phase 2b trial in over 500 subjects, which in 2007 failed to separate from placebo on its primary efficacy endpoint. The obesity programme was wound down, and the detailed phase 2b results were never published in a peer-reviewed journal - so the negative result is both the most informative fact about the compound and the least accessible one.

That history is routinely presented backwards. Material promoting it cites the phase 2a figures and the mechanism and omits the larger, longer trial that did not replicate them. A failed phase 2b in five hundred people is stronger evidence than a positive phase 2a in three hundred, not weaker, and it is the reason no regulator has approved AOD-9604 for obesity or for anything else.

The compounding record follows the same line. It was placed in Category 2 of the FDA's interim 503A bulks list in September 2023 and removed in September 2024 on nominator withdrawal - again a withdrawal rather than a clearance - and in December 2024 the FDA determined that neither the free base nor the acetate should be included on the 503A Bulks List, citing limited long-term safety data, peptide impurities and potential immunogenicity. It has also been claimed as having food-ingredient status, which is a separate regulatory pathway and says nothing about efficacy as a drug.
monographs.offLabelUses: Marketed for fat loss despite negative trial results.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Not approved as a medicine.

monographs.summary: Androgen. A controlled substance in the US; prescription-only.
monographs.body: Testosterone replacement is a well-established therapy when prescribed for diagnosed deficiency, with established monitoring requirements — haematocrit, PSA where relevant, and lipids.
monographs.offLabelUses: Widely used outside prescribed indications for body composition and performance.
monographs.safetyNotes: Raises haematocrit; suppresses natural production and fertility while used. Requires monitoring, which is the part most often skipped when it is obtained outside a prescription.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Prescription-only; Schedule III controlled substance in the US.

monographs.summary: Adrenal steroid precursor, sold over the counter in the US as a supplement.
monographs.body: DHEA is a precursor that the body converts into other steroid hormones, so its effects are not confined to one pathway.
monographs.safetyNotes: It is prohibited in most competitive sport. Being a hormone precursor, it can influence oestrogen and androgen levels.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Sold as a dietary supplement in the US; a controlled substance in several other countries.

monographs.summary: Thyroid hormone replacement. Prescription-only, and unusually sensitive to what else is taken alongside it.
monographs.body: Levothyroxine absorption is markedly reduced by calcium, iron, and some other minerals, which is why separation in time matters more for this than for most medicines.
monographs.safetyNotes: Calcium and iron supplements taken close together with it can substantially reduce its absorption — a common and easily missed cause of an unstable thyroid level.
monographs.regulatoryStatus: Prescription-only.
